title: Coming home
hookLine: crossing the threshold with a blessing
tomorrow: what's so holy about a table of pasta and spilled water?

lines: THE DAY WALKS IN BEHIND YOU.
A LITTLE BOWL BY THE DOOR.
A FEW SECONDS ON THE THRESHOLD.
cards: Keys in the lock. The bag hits the floor. And sometimes the whole day walks in right behind you: the boss's tone, the rude customer, the group chat, and it lands on whoever happens to be in the kitchen.

Some Catholic homes keep a small holy water font by the front door, a little bowl on the wall at about hand height. Fingers in, the sign of the cross, then inside. A few seconds on the threshold, before the day gets in.

teach.b: Where does that come from? In Luke, when Jesus sends his disciples out to the towns, he gives them words for every doorway. In the Douay-Rheims: "Into whatsoever house you enter, first say: Peace be to this house."
First, before anything else. Then a detail that's easy to miss. If nobody there receives that peace, he says, it isn't wasted.
It comes back to the one who offered it. In the Gospels, doorways are where things arrive.
Jesus walks into the house of Zacchaeus, a tax collector the crowd grumbled about, and says, "This day is salvation come to this house." Catholic custom keeps the threshold in small ways.
Holy water by the door is a sacramental: not a sacrament, the Catechism says, but a sign that prepares a person to receive grace.
The sign of the cross that goes with it carries words from the end of Matthew: "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost."
So what does this give someone after a bad day? A line on the floor.
On one side, the day. On the other, the people you live with, or the quiet you live in. A blessing at the door is a way of choosing what crosses with you, and what stays on the step.

how: Some Catholic families keep a holy water font by the front door and make the sign of the cross with it coming and going; a priest can also be asked to bless a home.

o: a soldier's return after a long time away
moving back in with your parents as an adult
crossing back through your own door with a blessing

games.q: at the door — tap the pairs.
p: words from the end of Matthew

s: holy water by the door counts as a sacrament
the Catechism calls it a sacramental, a sign that prepares a person to receive grace.
in Luke, peace nobody receives comes back to the one who offered it
Jesus told the disciples to greet only houses that welcomed them
peace comes first, at whatever house they enter.

games.q: your roommate comes in slamming the door after a terrible shift, and you've had one too. by Luke's doorway, what goes first?
o: peace first: a real greeting before either of you unloads.
the complaints first, to clear the air quickly.
silence, and both of you head to your rooms.
games.why: Jesus says first say: peace be to this house. the day can come in after; the greeting goes first.

practice: Stand and face a doorway near you, any doorway. Stop on the line and let the last few hours drain out of your shoulders.
Then step through, with the sign of the cross if that's yours, or Luke's words under your breath: peace be to this house.

wordCard.voice: Coming home. Crossing back through your own door, and marking it with a blessing.

orig.note: Latin: peace to this house, Luke 10:5 in the Vulgate.

carryVoice: The line to keep: home blessed, with peace said first at the door. Rest well tonight.
